extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public administration; government administrators and organizational planners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on organizing line and staff relationships, managing administrative committees, and conducting program/management planning (steps, levels, procedural choices, and controls). Intended to help planners and administrators design effective organizational and planning machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff officer authority and divergent delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: The setting up of operating staff officers frequently involves a departure from strict scalar organization ... some agencies require staff officials to issue instructions over the signature of a line administrator. But others frankly recognize divergent delegation and allow staff officers to issue instructions on their own responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that staff officers may need to give directions across line units for employment, purchasing, etc. Agencies must choose whether to preserve 'scalar' fiction (signatures of line administrators) or to allow staff officers independent authority; the choice affects accountability and practical operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionalism (centralization of administrative processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionalism holds that organization should go entirely by staff functions or processes, and that each process should be performed by a single unit for the whole organization ... All operations which overlap two or more fields ... are centralized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionalism is proclaimed to improve performance and avoid wasted time caused by slacks, but it must be evaluated in context: centralizing administrative processes (filing, drafting, planning, research, etc.) can improve efficiency but may produce nuisances for line officials (e.g., 'perfect' filing rooms that impede line work). Discussed further in chapter on 'work distribution.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of operating staff divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating staff divisions can justify themselves only by proving that their specialists can do their share of the work better — sufficiently so to compensate for additional administrative moves caused by shifting the sequences concerned from division to division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate staffing units on net effect: the end-result must be an improvement in quality and speed and a reduction in the cost of administration when considering both the specific operation and the entire administrative job.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions for deciding line vs staff balance
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no uniformly desirable compromise between pure line organization and the more advanced phases of staff organization ... In this connection there could be asked a few questions which are simple enough but which require thorough analysis of the situation to get the right answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these analytic questions to determine proper organization at each intersection of line function and staff function: (1) Which technique is dominant — line or staff? (2) Can the staff function be more economically performed by line or a specialized staff unit? Is the volume sufficient to justify a unit? (3) Will transferring work to staff delay line work, cause 'administrative pyramiding' or duplication, or complicate line duties? (4) Is the staff function so interrelated that line officers must exercise close technical supervision, or can they ignore it? (5) Are there administrative dangers (graft in purchasing, political influence in personnel) that make a staff unit useful for control? Answering these objectively, based on major purposes rather than formalism, determines proper organization and duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate committee type selection
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four main types of administrative committees: the executive committee (direct responsibilities, makes decisions, gives orders); the policy-forming or planning committee (analyzes and develops long-range programs; best to submit determinations as recommendations); the fact-finding committee (gathers and classifies information but usually does not recommend); and the discussion committee (exists mainly for exchanging information and ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the committee type according to the task: don't give policy-forming committees direct authority (submit recommendations to chief administrator to avoid confusion); expect committees to evolve or hybridize; choose committees only where jobs call for joint consideration across jurisdictions or reconciliation of discordant interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee management and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees tend to multiply, bog down if instructions are not specific, and overburden the busiest officials; therefore systematic management is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appoint one official with final authority over committee assignments to keep records of membership, duties, and accomplishments. Apply rules: forestall unnecessary committees; ensure each has a definite and limited assignment that does not duplicate other committees or hamper operating units; work out a time budget (hours/month including between-meeting work); control selection of members to avoid overload; arrange temporary assignment of research staff if needed; give junior executives opportunities for in-service training; and obtain brief but informative progress reports so committee work is accounted for in planning and coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning steps (definition, policies, program, design, differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harlow S. Person suggests that planning consists of successive steps: (1) definition of purpose, (2) formulation of policies (determining exact limits), (3) formulation of program (arranging ways and means in a tentative program), (4) design of plan (bringing ways and means into exact quantitative, qualitative, and functional relationships), and (5) differentiation of projects (making each as independent as possible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the first three steps as determining what is to be done (administrative/program planning) and the fourth and fifth as management/procedural planning (deciding how programs are carried out). Account for men/materials and organizational environment at each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of planning and scope (directive, administrative, operative; administrative vs management planning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Person differentiates planes of planning: (1) directive planning — making up a program, dividing into major projects with lump-sum budgets, control of broad policies; (2) administrative planning — assignment of tasks to specific working units and control by comparing accomplishment with plan; (3) operative planning — within working units. The text distinguishes 'administrative planning' (what is to be done) from 'management planning' (planning the administration of the activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At each level, address appropriate elements (Figure 12): directive (frame of organization, major fields, channels of responsibility, broad procedures); middle/admin (assignment to subordinate units, more specific procedures, timing/scheduling, means of observation/direction); operative (division into tasks, assignment to individuals, operating procedures, flow and timing, specification of group jobs, work budgets). Ensure planning and management planning occur across these planes but at appropriate detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-specification in planning
rubrics_metrics.description: "Neither administrative nor management planning should go too far into the technical details of operations. 'Detailed specification,' says Dr. Person, 'is a function of the technological methods necessary for the achievement of the objective, not of planning itself. Planning does not seek detail in arrangement for its own sake.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify methods only to the degree necessary to ensure execution of the plan. In management planning (office work) more detail may be required, but avoid unnecessary pre-arranging beyond technological needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of planning responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A plan begins with an idea ... the initial responsibility for planning means the responsibility for gathering ideas, sifting them, and putting the good ones in usable form. The top administrator cannot delegate the responsibility of evaluating the plan in its broad aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure planning responsibility is distributed appropriately: program planning is a line function and remains the responsibility of top administrators and division chiefs for broad evaluation and feasibility; while parts of planning/execution may be delegated, the final evaluation of broad aspects rests with the top administrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous cycle of planning, execution, control, and replanning
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning, as a continuous process, begins with the assembling of data needed to determine objectives and means of accomplishment ... There is thus a continuous cycle of planning, execution, control, and re-planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base planning on operating experience and data collected through clearances, inspections, reports, accounts, and similar administrative controls; treat planning as iterative across directive/administrative/operative planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select planning procedure according to trade-offs (speed, accuracy, acceptability, coordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are alternative ways of planning, the choice depending on administrative need. If time is short but dovetailing not vital, have individuals or small groups prepare plans with direction only in terms of major policies. If close coordination is vital, have a central planning authority (but avoid over-involvement). If acceptability is most important, planning by line executives or networks of committees is preferable though slow and occasionally inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a compromise based on the relative importance of different objectives — rarely can planning embody high speed, perfect technical accuracy, extreme acceptability, and complete coordination all at once. Adjust planning machinery accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder involvement for acceptability and practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: The program of integrated land-use planning by USDA is an example where democratic planning by farmers themselves was essential because compulsion was repugnant; having farmers do much of the planning produced plans more likely to be workable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When plans affect many actors (e.g., farmers, local communities), involve those directly concerned (local committees, stakeholders) to secure acceptability and workable results; combine local planning with technical assistance and state/federal review to integrate into broader program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design stage for joint programs: allocation, negotiation, drafting, promulgation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design — deciding who does what, when, and where — often translates plans into schedules through interbureau conferences; the Office acts as secretariat preparing agenda and information, conferees act as technical advisors and negotiators, minutes summarize conclusions and points remaining at issue, a schedule is agreed upon, drafted in exact form, and promulgated by the Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For interbureau or multi-agency programs, ensure a coordinating office (secretariat) prepares agendas, information, and minutes; require bureaus to indicate feasibility and what they will do; negotiate schedules, draft exact operating plans, and formally promulgate them to ensure acceptance and clarity of execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency rapid centralized planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the Department is faced with a situation demanding immediate and positive action, a short-cut planning procedure is used: planning begins in the Bureau which sends investigators to examine the problem and keeps the essential work within its own hands. By thus controlling the time element a complete operating plan can be worked up to meet a close deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In emergencies, use centralized, rapid planning within a capable bureau or small group to control time and produce an actionable plan; reserve the slower, participatory bottom-up procedures for non-urgent, permanent planning.
